newsitem.title: USA: U.S. high court sides with Texaco in oil tax case.
newsitem.headline: U.S. high court sides with Texaco in oil tax case.

text.p: The U.S. Supreme Court Monday rejected an Internal Revenue Service appeal in a dispute with Texaco Inc. over what the federal agency calculated to be more than $1 billion in taxes on Saudi Arabian oil.
The U.S. Justice Department, in appealing to the high court on behalf of the IRS, said more than $2 billion also was at stake in a companion tax case involving Exxon Corp.

But the Supreme Court denied the government's appeal without comment or dissent, letting stand a U.S. appeals court ruling for Texaco in a case that dates back to the Saudi Arabian oil policy for 1979-81.
Texaco said later it expected to receive a refund of $700 million as a result of the court's decision, mostly this year. Mobil Corp. said it also expected a $700 million refund.
Texaco disputed the government's figure on the amount due, saying the actual asserted tax deficiency involved $800 million.
A 1979 letter by the Saudi Arabian oil minister had required that Texaco and other members of the Arabian American Oil Co. (Aramco) re-sell Saudi Arabian crude oil at specified. below-market prices.

The IRS contended that a Texaco domestic subsidiary which acted as an international trading company in reselling the oil unduly shifted profits to its foreign affiliates for the 1979-81 tax years. The IRS increased the subsidiary's U.S. taxable income to reflect those profits.
A U.S. Tax Court held that the 1979 Saudi policy bars the IRS from using its authority to reallocate the income, a position upheld by the appeals court in October.
The appeals court accepted Texaco's argument that it had no power to control the allocation of profits on Saudi oil because of the restrictions imposed by the 1979 letter.

The Justice Department in its appeal argued that the case "presents an issue of exceptional fiscal and administrative importance." It said the directive of a foreign government should not bar the IRS from apportioning or allocating gross income involving the affiliate of a U.S. firm.

Texaco replied that the Saudi government was exercising its sovereign powers in issuing the 1979 restriction and that it had acted at the urging of the U.S. government, which was concerned at the time about soaring world oil prices.
Exxon also urged that the government's appeal in the Texaco case be rejected, saying there was no justification for further Supreme Court review of the fact-bound dispute.
Texaco stock rose 75 cents to $104.375, Exxon dropped 12.5 cents to $53.375 and Mobil fell 87.5 cents to $125.625, all in consolidated trading on the New York Stock Exchange.
